item.title: New Scientist: Will the backlash against AI data centres hit quantum computing too?
item.description: To succeed at scale, quantum computing must differentiate itself from AI, says columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan. But the two technologies are already mixed up in the eyes of the public

item.title: New Scientist: I am a top drone pilot in the Ukrainian Army – this is what it is really like
item.description: Kratos is the call sign of one of the leading drone pilots in Ukraine. As part of the Aquila regiment, 3rd Army Corps, he has taken down almost 1000 enemy drones

item.title: Nature: Can pancreatic cancer be stopped in its tracks? Radical tactic raises hopes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03119-7 With prospects for new treatments at an all-time high, researchers are looking for ways to boost survival by treating the disease early.

item.title: Nature: A black hole’s jets have a halo effect
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03036-9 Observations confirm jets’ expected effect on the gas cloud that surrounds a galaxy.

item.title: New Scientist: Earth’s geographic poles wander more than we had thought
item.description: A phenomenon known as true polar wander, different to the movement of the magnetic poles, may be more common and more dramatic than previously known

item.title: New Scientist: Ukraine rolls out drone-stopping razor fence to thwart attacks
item.description: Most of the drones being used by Russia in the war with Ukraine are controlled by cables several tens of kilometres long. A new defensive tool cuts the cables to stop the drones

item.title: Nature: Sign of the times: AI lingo muscles into esteemed dictionary
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03044-9 ‘Agentic’, ‘prompt engineering’ and other technical terms are among the 1,400 entries added to Merriam-Webster’s online catalogue.

item.title: New Scientist: Elephants imitate each other when they produce deep rumbling sounds
item.description: African savannah elephants use a variety of calls to communicate, and now machine learning has shown that they tune their deepest sounds to match those of other nearby elephants

item.title: Nature: Retraction Note: Ribosomal frameshifting in the CCR5 mRNA is regulated by miRNAs and the NMD pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11149-4 Retraction Note: Ribosomal frameshifting in the CCR5 mRNA is regulated by miRNAs and the NMD pathway

item.title: New Scientist: Placenta wrap hastens erection recovery after prostate surgery
item.description: Dried amniotic membranes from donated placentas can be wrapped around delicate nerves during prostate cancer surgery to hasten the time to a first erection after the procedure

item.title: ScienceDaily: This giant stick insect fooled scientists for decades
item.description: Scientists have identified two new species of large Australian stick insects, including one that lays extraordinary “lidded” eggs never before recorded in the group. The discovery also revealed that a familiar stick insect had been misidentified for decades, showing how much biodiversity may still be hiding in plain sight.

item.title: ScienceDaily: New “plant armor” more than triples strawberry yields
item.description: A new protective fabric boosted strawberry yields by as much as 3.56 times while blocking insects and still allowing sunlight, rain, and airflow to reach the plants. Originally inspired by research on military clothing, Plant Armor could also help farms reduce pesticide and water use.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
item.description: A proposed qubit made with superfluid helium could cut quantum computing error rates by around 100 times by shielding quantum information from common forms of electromagnetic noise. If experiments confirm the predictions, the technology could eventually work alongside today’s superconducting qubits or serve as a new kind of quantum memory.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy
item.description: UCLA researchers built an AI system that uses light to analyze more than a dozen videos simultaneously, detecting deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy. Its speed, low energy demands, and resistance to attacks could make it a powerful tool for screening the growing flood of AI-generated video.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
item.description: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

item.title: ScienceDaily: 1 in 13 adults under 30 already had hidden artery plaque
item.description: More than half of 16,000 apparently healthy adults had signs of atherosclerosis, with arterial plaques already detectable in about 1 in 13 people ages 18 to 29. Researchers say directly imaging the arteries could reveal hidden cardiovascular disease years or even decades before symptoms appear.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
item.description: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
item.description: The Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may actively damage brain blood vessels and sabotage the cellular systems that remove harmful proteins. Researchers were able to reverse some of these effects in experiments, revealing promising new targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and other neurodegenerative diseases.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Caltech physicists finally measure a quantum energy ladder predicted 40 years ago
item.description: Researchers have experimentally observed energy patterns that physicists have predicted for about 40 years. By arranging laser-trapped atoms into a quantum simulator, they recreated two different quantum tipping points and watched the atoms fall into the exact energy ratios predicted by theory. The technique could now be used to explore mysterious quantum systems where scientists do not already know the answer.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This common mistake can add nearly 7 points to your blood pressure reading
item.description: A common mistake during blood pressure checks could make readings appear substantially higher than they really are. Johns Hopkins researchers found that leaving the arm unsupported can raise systolic readings by about 6.5 mmHg, potentially affecting a hypertension diagnosis.

item.title: New Scientist: The best popular-science books of October 2026
item.description: With a new book from the late primatologist Frans de Waal and a deep dive into artificial intelligence from New York Times tech columnist Kevin Roose, there is some hard-hitting popular science to look forward to this month – with added Pokémon, says Liz Else

item.title: Nature: Gaze into the cosmos and through the eyes of a bee — September’s best science images
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03101-3 The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

item.title: Nature: Battle of the Anthropocene: allegations re-ignite row over proposed geologic epoch
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03118-8 Researchers say that a vote to reject the epoch violated procedure and call for transparency.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: How to save corals from the El Niño
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03138-4 Scientists are trying to help coral reefs survive record ocean temperatures. Plus, the aftermath of a deadly attack on Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and whether it’s OK to dodge small talk.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Vaping has ‘alarming’ risks for children
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03122-y Vaping in childhood comes with bigger health risks than we thought. Plus, chemists can’t seem to ditch hazardous solvents and whether apocalyptic claims about AI are a dangerous distraction.

item.title: New Scientist: A lack of rockets is creating a crisis for space technology companies
item.description: SpaceX’s changing priorities, the war in Ukraine and a lack of competitors are all causing a launch crisis that might last years

item.title: New Scientist: Can mathematicians still refuse to use AI at this point?
item.description: There’s no question AI has transformed the field of mathematics in the past few months. Columnist Jacob Aron wonders if it will soon be impossible to be an AI refusenik and continue working in the field

item.title: Nature: The 'missed disease' that affects 190 million: endometriosis drug shows early promise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03042-x Modified medication targets the cells implicated in the condition's tell-tale lesions.

item.title: New Scientist: Anglo-Saxons got special treatment in medieval Rome
item.description: A small hoard of medieval English coins found near the Vatican in Rome suggests that early English residents held a privileged status in the holy city

item.title: Nature: This award-winning microscopy image used AI — igniting controversy in a prestigious competition
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03086-z Researchers say that using artificial-intelligence tools to visualize scientific images can become problematic when models misrepresent the underlying data.

item.title: Nature: AI ‘speech clock’ assesses how fast you’re ageing from your voice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03106-y The pitch and emotional content of your speech are important predictors of accelerated ageing, researchers find.

item.description: The September read for the New Scientist Book Club was a challenging trip to the edges of space-time with Chanda Prescod-Weinstein – but one which most book club members thoroughly enjoyed

item.title: New Scientist: This week’s new questions
item.description: Why do dogs generally follow instructions, whereas cats largely ignore them? Will we ever build a space telescope that can see as far as the big bang?

item.title: New Scientist: Why a modern approach to healthcare must consider more than illness
item.description: Pills and other medications may seem like the most rigorous way to treat illness, but we increasingly know that our health must revolve around the whole mind and body

item.title: New Scientist: A ‘unique opportunity’: is this the weirdest RightMove listing ever?
item.description: Feedback is a little saddened to discover that a historic scientific building is up for sale, and wonders if any readers fancy opening a museum

item.title: New Scientist: Why do we have hair – on our heads and elsewhere? A new book explores
item.description: Judy Wearing's Anxious and Hairy is an enthusiastic and curious dive into the evolution and culture of human hair. An initially sceptical Elle Hunt is captivated

item.title: New Scientist: Moonfish, a haunting animation, captures a tragedy in space
item.description: Daniel Zvereff’s animation, Moonfish, exposes the grief-filled and strange reality of space miner Cassius’s life working on an asteroid after things go tragically wrong. Drawn in black and white, it’s a tiny budget wonder

item.title: New Scientist: Unsettling images reveal stark impact of humans on the environment
item.description: These aerial shots from photographer and environmental activist J. Henry Fair, drawn from a new exhibition, show the impact of human activity on the landscape

item.title: New Scientist: Benjamin Labatut has written an utterly haunting novella about science
item.description: Using real scientists as characters, When We Cease to Understand the World looks at what happens when science unravels the conceit that we can understand reality. It is a brilliant piece of writing, says Jacklin Kwan

item.title: Nature: Who’s the loudest of them all? The bare-throated bellbird vies for the prize
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03038-7 The bellbird’s extra-large gape helps it to achieve pneumatic-drill-level volume.

item.title: Nature: How did Earth get its water? Inside the extreme machine seeking answers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02978-4 The Z machine in New Mexico generates shockwaves that can simulate conditions deep inside our planet.

item.title: Nature: Secret watermark labels proteins as ‘made by AI’
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03033-y An innovative safeguard could help to flag proteins devised by artificial-intelligence tools such as AlphaFold, but the digital marker can be erased.

item.title: Nature: Population-scale immune multiome atlas reveals regulatory disease mechanisms
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11078-2 Population-scale simultaneous profiling of chromatin accessibility and gene expression across immune cells reveals regulatory architectures that connect genetic variants to disease.

item.title: New Scientist: Slashing sugar intake before antibiotics may save your microbiome
item.description: Antibiotics can reduce the diversity of microbes in your gut and lead to health problems, but a study in people with cancer has identified a potential solution

item.title: New Scientist: The overlooked power of diet for improving your mental health
item.description: Therapy and drugs are the go-to options for improving mental health. But psychologist Kimberley Wilson argues that what we eat also has a crucial role to play

item.title: Nature: These optical illusions are whybutterflies are so hard to catch
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03124-w High-speed footage of takeoffs reveal that the butterfly markings mislead the eye, making them harder to catch.

item.title: Nature: 2D semiconductor aims to turbocharge development of high-performance electronics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02777-x An ultrathin semiconductor that conducts electricity using positively charged ‘holes’ might clear the way for next-generation electronic devices.

item.title: Nature: Elena, Aris, Marcus: AI-generated ‘ghosts’ are polluting the scientific literature
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02991-7 The overuse of certain names has revealed the scale of fake experts on academic publishing platforms, say researchers.

item.title: Nature: Sugar amplifies antibiotic disruption of gut microbes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02782-0 People who underwent stem-cell transplantation and ate sugar-rich food had disrupted communities of gut microorganisms during antibiotic treatment.

item.title: Nature: Harmful tau spreads like self-propagating prion proteins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02778-w Structural studies support the idea that fibrillized tau protein, a feature of neurodegenerative disorders, acts as a prion-like template to induce misfolding in healthy tau.

item.title: Nature: Pipework problems when cancer spreads to an area bordering the brain
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02783-z Analysis of cancer growing adjacent to the brain reveals that bone-eroding cells interfere with lymphatic drainage vessels and hinder anti-tumour immune responses.

item.title: Nature: Sugar-rich foods exacerbate antibiotic-induced microbiome disruption
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11077-3 Avoiding a diet rich in simple sugars during treatment with antibiotics may mitigate microbiota disruption.

item.title: Nature: Type 2 immune history trains lung macrophages for viral disease tolerance
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11060-y Type 2 inflammation trains nerve- and airway-associated macrophages to confer disease tolerance against lethal influenza by limiting immunopathology and promoting tissue repair without enhancing viral clearance.

item.title: Nature: Global mangrove distribution on the open coast is controlled by waves
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11089-z A process-driven mangrove presence or absence model using 20 years of open-source wave data shows that wave conditions are critical in determining where mangroves grow worldwide.

item.title: Nature: X-ray liquidography decodes complex motions in azobenzene isomerization
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11068-4 Time-resolved X-ray liquidography films the structural changes of azobenzene during trans-to-cis isomerization in solution with atomic-level precision.

item.title: Nature: Histone readers MLLT1 and MLLT3 concentrate AID to confer locus specificity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11087-1 By being restricted to target regions by MLLT1–MLLT3 occupancy, activation-induced deaminase activity is able to avoid most off-target mutagenesis during B cell somatic hypermutation.

item.title: Nature: Carbene transfer from thianthrenium ylides for cyclopropanation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11108-z Thianthrenium ylides can be used as a general platform for metal–carbene generation and transfer, including cyclopropanation, σ-bond insertion and sigmatropic rearrangements.

item.title: Nature: An amygdala to anterior hypothalamic circuit gates stress sensitivity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11075-5 The anterior hypothalamic nucleus regulates negative valence in the brain, highlighting a new pathway that controls sensitivity to stressful events and signposting approaches to identify new circuit interactions relevant to mental health.

item.title: Nature: Dynamic protrusions mediate crawling motility in Asgard archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11063-9 Anoxic live-cell imaging shows actin-dependent crawling motility and dynamic protrusions in Asgard archaea, providing insights into cellular innovations that may have contributed to eukaryotic evolution.

item.title: Nature: Osteoclasts intercept meningeal lymphatic paths for dural metastasis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11082-6 Osteoclast-derived angiopoietin-2 in the dura mater impairs lymphatic vessel function and weakens anti-tumour immunity against dural metastases, which offers new therapeutic approaches to restore meningeal lymphatic function through selective osteoclast targeting.

item.title: Nature: Human genetics implicates a BACH2–NRF2 axis in fetal haemoglobin activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11113-2 BACH2 restrains activation of the fetal-haemoglobin-encoding γ-globin genes, while loss of BACH2 enhances NRF2 chromatin occupancy and promotes the formation of activation foci at the γ-globin genes.

item.title: Nature: Prion-like transmission of human tau strains in the mouse brain
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11061-x Mouse experiments show that Alzheimer’s disease and corticobasal degeneration tau filaments retain their distinct structures during templated seeding, supporting strain-specific tau propagation and disease modelling.

item.title: Nature: Wafer-scale epitaxy growth of high-mobility p-type boron carbon nitride
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11047-9 A dual-precursor chemical system is used to achieve wafer-scale epitaxy growth of boron carbon nitride, a high-performance p-type semiconductor, for potential integration in efficient 2D materials for electronics.

item.title: Nature: Written in development and lost in ageing: the grammar of cellular identity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10955-0 Ageing reflects progressive decanalization of mammalian cell identity, driven by erosion of a regulatory grammar written during development.

item.title: Nature: Transcription pause and elongation regulators mediate somatic hypermutation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11092-4 The molecular factors and mechanisms that mediate the chromatin recruitment of activation-induced deaminase and the generation of its stalled polymerase II substrate during somatic hypermutation are identified.

item.title: Nature: GPCR antagonism via rewiring of receptor trafficking and degradation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11088-0 A strategy for functional G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) antagonism through bispecific antibody-mediated endocytosis and lysosomal degradation is reported.

item.title: Nature: γδ T cell receptor dependencies define a unique immunosurveillance modality
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11076-4 Tissue-resident γδ T cells mount rapid, innate-like stress responses that require γδ T cell receptor signalling, revealing lineage-specific receptor dependence that underpins their conserved roles in immunosurveillance and informs therapeutic deployment.

item.title: Nature: Spatiotemporal clonal architecture of the newborn mouse forebrain
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11064-8 Clonal barcoding across the newborn mouse forebrain reveals developmental principles whereby glutamatergic neurons and astrocytes remain locally derived, whereas widely dispersed GABAergic (γ-aminobutyric acid-producing) lineages link neurons with oligodendrocyte precursor cells.

item.title: Nature: Scalable decision-making for games of imperfect information
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11036-y Ataraxos, an AI for the board wargame Stratego, establishes a design pattern for reinforcement learning and search that is effective under large amounts of hidden information, a longstanding desideratum of the field of strategic decision-making.

item.title: Nature: Evolution of terrestrial anatomy revealed by a derived stem tetrapod
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11090-6 New anatomical evidence reclassifies Westlothiana as an aquatic stem tetrapod, showing that terrestrial limb adaptations evolved mosaically in transitional amphibious environments before crown tetrapods emerged.

item.title: Nature: Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11062-w Butterfly wing patterns and flight dynamics work in tandem to create powerful visual illusions that confuse predators, potentially representing one of the most successful visual defence strategies in moving animals.

item.title: Nature: Self-aligned optical microcomb emerging between octave-separated lasers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11086-2 An architectural inversion shifts integrated optical frequency comb generation from outward broadening around a central pump to filling the spectrum between two octave-separated pumps through a self-aligned parametrically driven cavity soliton, enabling robust self-referencing for future deployable on-chip frequency and time metrology.

item.title: Nature: Function-preserving watermarking of AI-generated proteins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10965-y SynthIDBio watermarks AI-generated protein sequences and structures while preserving function, enabling provenance detection and offering a proof-of-concept tool for biosecurity and information integrity.

item.title: Nature: A TBK1/ULK1 signalling axis couples lysosomal stress to TFEB activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11093-3 Proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses of lysosomes identify a nutrient-independent regulatory arm of mTORC1 signalling that mediates lysosomal adaptation to stress and whose deregulation underlies tumorigenesis in follicular lymphoma.

item.title: Nature: A two-hit mechanism triggers autoimmune hair loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11098-y Immune dysregulation and physiological neural activation converge to trigger autoimmune alopecia.

item.title: New Scientist: ‘Astonishing’ weight loss when GLP-1 drug used with second medication
item.description: Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, is our most potent weight-loss drug, but it can be made even more effective when combined with a complementary medicine

item.title: ScienceDaily: Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
item.description: A review of more than 265,000 people found that cannabis use was associated with higher rates of both committing violence and becoming a victim of it. The researchers say the link is significant but does not prove cannabis itself is the cause.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
item.description: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Ocean heatwaves are hiding months of extra warming
item.description: Marine heatwaves may be only the most intense part of much longer warming events, with elevated temperatures sometimes lingering for months. Researchers found that conventional measurements underestimate total heat exposure by more than 150% on average, potentially overlooking a major source of stress on marine ecosystems.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Mulberry may reshape gut bacteria and influence metabolism
item.description: Mulberry compounds may reshape the gut microbiome in ways that support intestinal health and metabolism, with some combinations showing especially strong effects in animal studies. However, the results vary depending on the plant part and processing method, and the benefits have yet to be confirmed in humans.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
item.description: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
item.description: Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Pompeii’s 2,000-year-old eruption just gave scientists a better clock for Earth’s past
item.description: Mount Vesuvius’ famous 79 CE eruption has given scientists a remarkably precise benchmark for dating events deep in Earth’s past. The improved technique could sharpen the timelines of volcanic eruptions, asteroid impacts, extinctions, and other major moments in geological history.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Watch Live: NASA’s Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
item.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1. The Dragon could reach the orbiting laboratory in just 7 hours and 50 minutes, making it the fastest U.S. spacecraft journey to the ISS in history.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Bats may have first evolved in Europe 65 million years ago
item.description: A huge genomic and fossil study suggests bats first evolved in Europe around 65 to 60 million years ago before spreading across the globe. The findings also indicate that flight and echolocation emerged near the beginning of bat evolution, potentially helping explain how bats became one of the most successful mammal groups on Earth.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
item.description: NASA’s Curiosity rover marked 5,000 Martian days by capturing morning and afternoon views that were blended into a striking Mars “postcard.” The panorama shows Curiosity, its tracks, and the enormous landscape surrounding Mount Sharp and Gale Crater.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
item.description: Wild blacktip sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from nearly 250 feet away, according to experiments conducted off the Florida coast. The sharks not only heard the sounds but sharply changed direction away from them, suggesting they could pinpoint where they were coming from.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Creatine may help build muscle even without exercise, researchers find
item.description: Creatine helped middle-aged adults gain muscle and strength even without a structured workout program in a new 12-week study. When combined with exercise and a calorie-reduced diet, it produced even greater strength gains while helping participants add lean tissue and lose fat. Researchers say the results strengthen the case for creatine as a potentially useful tool for maintaining muscle with age.

item.title: Nature: Is exposomics the key to making personalized medicine a reality?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02958-8 Scientists say tailored disease treatments require a comprehensive assessment of a person’s lifelong environmental exposures.

item.title: Nature: How to spend $25 billion on science: OpenAI’s staggeringly rich research charity gets under way
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03015-0 Jacob Trefethen, who leads life sciences at the OpenAI Foundation, speaks to Nature about the organization’s ambitions to cure disease.

item.title: Nature: Restoring hearing in people with a rare form of deafness
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02894-7 How a decades-long quest led to the first gene therapy for deafness caused by a mutation.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Forget LASIK: Safer, cheaper vision correction without lasers or incisions
item.description: Scientists are developing a possible alternative to LASIK that reshapes the cornea without cutting it or using a laser. The technique uses a small electric potential and a specially shaped platinum lens to temporarily soften the cornea, allowing it to be molded in about a minute.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces
item.description: Depression may change which emotional faces children notice most, but the pattern appears to depend on family history. Children at higher familial risk became increasingly focused on sad faces, while lower-risk children with rising symptoms paid less attention to happy ones.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Quantum teleportation breakthrough: Scientists crack a 25-year entanglement challenge
item.description: Scientists have developed and experimentally demonstrated a long-sought method for identifying W states, an important form of multi-photon quantum entanglement. The technique could make complex entangled systems much easier to measure, opening new possibilities for quantum teleportation, communication, and computing.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This 245-million-year-old fossil still has its stomach and intestines
item.description: A 245-million-year-old marine reptile fossil preserves an astonishing amount of detail, including its stomach, liver, and intestines. The discovery reveals that Austronaga minuta was highly adapted for swimming even though its digestive system remained surprisingly simple.
